articles.title: What to Do After Someone Dies: A Complete Checklist for the First 30 Days
articles.metaTitle: What to Do After Someone Dies: Checklist for 30 Days
articles.metaDescription: A step-by-step checklist for the first 30 days after a death — from the first phone calls to notifying banks, benefits, and closing accounts.
articles.body:
Losing someone is disorienting enough without also being handed a list of logistics no one prepares you for. This guide walks through what actually needs to happen in the first days and weeks after a death — organized by urgency, not by paperwork type, so you can focus on what matters most first.

If you'd rather answer a few questions and get a checklist built specifically for your situation, [After Atlas's guided checklist tool](/survey/death) does that in about 10 minutes. This guide covers the same ground in article form.

## The first 24–48 hours

**1. Get a legal pronouncement of death.** If the death didn't happen in a hospital or under hospice care, you may need to call 911 or the local medical examiner first. A funeral home generally cannot proceed without this.

**2. Contact a funeral home or crematorium.** If the person had prearranged plans, this step is largely already decided. If not, you'll need to choose one — most will guide you through the next several steps, including obtaining the death certificate.

**3. Notify immediate family.** Close family and anyone who should hear the news directly, before it circulates elsewhere.

**4. Arrange for care of dependents and pets.** If the person cared for children, an elderly relative, or animals, someone needs to step in immediately — this can't wait.

**5. Secure the home.** Lock up the property, and if it will sit empty, consider notifying neighbors or a security service, especially if valuables are inside.

## Within the first week

**6. Order certified copies of the death certificate.** Order more than you think you'll need — banks, insurers, and government agencies each typically require their own original copy. Ten to fifteen is a reasonable starting number for most estates.

**7. Locate the will (if one exists).** Check with the person's attorney, a safe deposit box, or a fireproof home safe. If there's no will, the estate will generally be distributed according to state intestate succession law, which determines who inherits without one.

**8. Identify the personal representative or executor.** This is the person legally authorized to manage the estate — either named in the will or, without a will, typically the closest next of kin willing to serve. This person will be the point of contact for most of what follows.

**9. Notify the person's employer**, if they were still working — for final pay, unused paid time off, and any employer-provided benefits like group life insurance.

**10. Contact Social Security**, if applicable, to report the death and stop future benefit payments (overpayments can complicate the estate later).

## Within the first two to four weeks

**11. Notify financial institutions**, including banks, brokerage and retirement accounts, and any lenders. For a full breakdown of what to expect from creditors and how debt is actually handled, see [our guide to what happens to debt when someone dies](/blog/what-happens-to-debt-when-someone-dies).

**12. File any life insurance claims.** Most insurers require a certified death certificate and a claim form; payouts commonly take a few weeks once filed.

**13. Cancel or transfer recurring expenses** — credit cards, subscriptions, memberships, and utilities, so charges don't continue accumulating.

**14. Handle digital accounts.** Email, cloud storage, social media, and any accounts holding money (PayPal, Venmo, cryptocurrency) each need their own approach. See [our guide to managing digital assets after a death](/blog/digital-assets-after-death-guide) for specifics.

**15. Decide what to do with the home and vehicles.** This often takes longer than everything else on this list — there's rarely a need to rush a decision here.

**16. Begin the probate process, if required.** Whether probate is necessary depends heavily on state law and how the estate's assets are titled. If you're in Washington State, see [our guide to whether you need probate](/blog/do-you-need-probate-in-washington-state) for the specific thresholds that apply.

## Don't forget: taking care of yourself

Somewhere in the middle of all of this, it's easy to put your own needs last. Grief doesn't pause for paperwork, and burnout during this period is common. If you have children in the household, they're processing this loss too — [here's guidance on supporting grieving children](/blog/helping-children-grieve-loss-family-member).

## Frequently asked questions

**How long do I have to handle everything after a death?**
There's no single deadline — some tasks (like notifying Social Security) are time-sensitive, while others (like selling a home) can reasonably take months. Prioritize by urgency rather than trying to do everything at once.

**Do I need a lawyer to do any of this?**
Not always. Many estates, especially smaller ones or those with a valid will and cooperative heirs, can be handled without a probate attorney. Larger, contested, or more complex estates usually benefit from one.

**What's the very first thing I should do?**
Get a legal pronouncement of death and contact a funeral home — nearly everything else follows from there.

---

articles.title: Do You Need Probate in Washington State? A Simple Guide
articles.metaTitle: Do You Need Probate in Washington State? A Simple Guide
articles.metaDescription: Learn when probate is required in Washington State, the $100,000 small estate affidavit threshold, and how community property changes the picture.
articles.body:
One of the first practical questions families face after a death is whether the estate has to go through probate at all. In Washington, the answer depends on how much the person owned, how it was titled, and whether they were married. Here's how to figure out where your situation falls.

## What probate actually is

Probate is the court-supervised process of validating a will (if there is one), paying the deceased person's debts, and legally transferring their assets to heirs. Washington handles this through the Superior Court in the county where the person lived — the state doesn't have a separate probate court.

Many Washington estates qualify for **nonintervention powers**, which let the personal representative administer and close the estate without ongoing court supervision — this is the norm for most solvent, uncontested estates, not the exception ([RCW 11.68.011](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=11.68.011)).

## When you likely don't need full probate

**The small estate affidavit.** If the total value of the decedent's probate assets is $100,000 or less, Washington law allows heirs to collect personal property using a small estate affidavit instead of going through probate — no court filing required ([RCW 11.62.010](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=11.62.010)). This process:

- Applies only to **personal property** (bank accounts, vehicles, personal belongings) — not real estate
- Can be used starting **40 days after the date of death**
- Is calculated on **net** value — outstanding debts and encumbrances are subtracted first
- Excludes the surviving spouse's own half of any community property, since that's already theirs

**Assets that pass outside probate entirely.** Some assets never enter the probate estate regardless of value, because they transfer automatically:
- Property held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship
- Accounts with a named payable-on-death or transfer-on-death beneficiary
- Life insurance and retirement accounts with a named beneficiary
- Assets held in a living trust

## When probate is likely required

- The estate includes **real estate** solely in the decedent's name (the small estate affidavit doesn't cover real property)
- Solely-owned financial accounts or other assets **exceed the $100,000 threshold**
- There's a **business interest** or other asset requiring formal legal authority to transfer
- There are **contested claims** — disputes among heirs, or creditors seeking payment through the estate
- A will exists that needs to be formally admitted

## How marriage changes the picture

Washington is a community property state ([RCW 26.16.030](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=26.16.030)), which affects probate in a specific way: if the deceased spouse's assets were entirely community property and there's no will (or a will leaving everything to the surviving spouse), that spouse's share often transfers automatically without probate, since the surviving spouse already owned half of it. Separate property — owned before the marriage, or received individually by gift or inheritance — is treated differently and may still require probate depending on its value and titling.

This is also where debt gets confusing for surviving spouses: responsibility for the deceased spouse's share of community debt generally passes to the surviving spouse along with their share of community assets. If you're navigating this, [our guide to what happens to debt after a death](/blog/what-happens-to-debt-when-someone-dies) covers it in more detail.

## What if there's no will?

Without a will, Washington's intestate succession laws determine who inherits, based on which relatives survive the decedent (spouse, children, parents, siblings, and so on) and whether the property is community or separate. The person handling the estate — typically the closest willing relative — becomes the de facto personal representative and may need to petition the court for that authority if probate is required.

## A rough timeline

There's no strict legal deadline to file for probate in Washington, but it's generally advisable to begin within 30 to 60 days of the death — both to protect estate assets and to start the formal creditor claims period, which limits how long creditors can come after the estate.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is $100,000 the total value of everything the person owned?**
No — it's the net value of probate assets only, after debts and encumbrances are subtracted, and excluding the surviving spouse's own community property share and anything that passes outside probate (like payable-on-death accounts).

**Can I do a small estate affidavit myself, without a lawyer?**
Many people do, since it doesn't require a court filing. That said, banks and other institutions sometimes require their own version of the form or additional documentation, so it's worth confirming requirements with each institution holding assets.

**Does owning a house always mean I need probate?**
Generally yes, if the house is solely in the decedent's name — the small estate affidavit doesn't cover real property. If it was held jointly with right of survivorship, or as community property with a surviving spouse, it may pass without probate.

*Thresholds and estate tax figures change over time — verify current numbers with the Washington Department of Revenue or a probate attorney before making decisions based on this article.*

## Sources

- [RCW 11.62.010](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=11.62.010) — Small estate affidavit statute, including the $100,000 threshold and 40-day waiting period
- [RCW 11.68.011](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=11.68.011) — Nonintervention powers for personal representatives
- [RCW 26.16.030](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=26.16.030) — Community property definition and management
- [Washington State Courts — Probate](https://www.courts.wa.gov/) — Superior Court jurisdiction over probate matters
- [Washington Department of Revenue — Estate Tax](https://dor.wa.gov/taxes-rates/other-taxes/estate-tax) — Current Washington estate tax exemption and rates

---

articles.title: What Happens to Debt When Someone Dies? What Washington Families Need to Know
articles.metaTitle: What Happens to Debt When Someone Dies? WA Families' Guide
articles.metaDescription: Do you inherit a loved one's debt? Here's how debt is actually handled after a death, and how Washington's community property law changes it.
articles.body:
If collection calls have started arriving for someone who's passed away, the first thing to know is this: in most cases, family members are not personally responsible for paying a deceased person's debts out of their own pocket ([Federal Trade Commission](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/debts-deceased-relatives)). Debt is generally the estate's responsibility, not the family's. Washington has one significant exception to this, described below, so it's worth reading through even if you've heard the general rule already.

## The general rule: debt belongs to the estate

When someone dies, their outstanding debts — credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, car loans — don't disappear, but they also don't automatically transfer to their children or other relatives. Instead:

1. The estate's personal representative identifies and notifies creditors
2. Creditors file claims against the estate within a set claims period
3. Valid debts are paid out of estate assets, in a specific order of priority (funeral costs and administration expenses typically come first, then secured debts, then unsecured debts)
4. Whatever remains after debts are paid goes to the heirs

If the estate doesn't have enough assets to cover everything, creditors generally don't get to collect from family members' own money — the debt is written off, with some exceptions below.

## The exceptions that do make you personally liable

The FTC and CFPB both confirm the same core exceptions ([FTC](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/debts-deceased-relatives)):

- **Co-signed debts.** If you co-signed a loan or credit card with the deceased, you're still responsible for it — this was true while they were alive and doesn't change at death.
- **Joint accounts.** If you were a joint account holder (not just an authorized user) on a credit card or loan, the same applies.
- **Continuing to use their credit.** If you keep using a deceased person's credit card after their death, you can become responsible for those new charges.

## Washington's community property exception

This is where Washington differs meaningfully from most of the country. Washington is one of a handful of community property states ([RCW 26.16.030](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=26.16.030)), meaning that debts incurred *during the marriage* are generally treated as belonging to both spouses jointly — not just the spouse who signed for them.

In practice, this means:

- A surviving spouse may be responsible for the deceased spouse's share of **community debt** — debt taken on during the marriage, even if only one spouse's name was on the account
- Debt from **before the marriage**, or debt that's clearly separate property, generally doesn't carry the same automatic exposure
- Creditors' claims are generally against **community assets and the surviving spouse's share of community property** — not against a surviving spouse's separate, pre-marital assets
- The probate process is what actually sorts out exactly what's owed and from what assets — this is one more reason probate (or a small estate affidavit) matters even when it feels like unnecessary paperwork. See [our guide to when probate is required in Washington](/blog/do-you-need-probate-in-washington-state) for the specifics.

If collection calls or letters are arriving quickly after a death, know that this is common and not necessarily a sign you owe anything yet — creditors are required to go through the estate's claims process, and it's reasonable to ask them to put things in writing rather than resolving anything over the phone in the moment.

## What to actually do

1. **Don't rush to pay anything from your own funds** before understanding whether you're actually obligated to.
2. **Get organized**: make a full list of the deceased person's debts, using statements, mail, and credit reports.
3. **Notify the three major credit bureaus** of the death, to prevent identity theft and stop new credit inquiries.
4. **Route creditor communication through the estate's probate process**, if one is opened, rather than negotiating individually and informally.
5. **Talk to a probate or family law attorney** if you're a surviving spouse and unsure whether a specific debt is community or separate — this distinction genuinely matters and isn't always obvious from the paperwork alone.

For the fuller picture of everything that needs handling after a death, not just debt, see [our complete first-30-days checklist](/blog/what-to-do-after-someone-dies-checklist).

## Frequently asked questions

**Do I inherit my parent's debt if they die?**
Generally no, unless you co-signed a loan with them or were a joint account holder. Their estate is responsible for their debts, not you personally.

**Is credit card debt forgiven when someone dies?**
Not forgiven exactly — it's paid from the estate's assets if there are enough, in order of priority. If the estate doesn't have enough assets, unsecured debt like most credit card debt is often simply not collectible from family members, outside of Washington's community property exception for spouses.

**What if my spouse died and I don't know what's community vs. separate debt?**
This is a genuinely common and reasonable point of confusion — it's worth a consultation with a Washington probate or family law attorney, since the distinction affects what a creditor can actually collect from you.

## Sources

- [Federal Trade Commission — Debts of Deceased Relatives](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/debts-deceased-relatives) — Who is (and isn't) personally responsible, and debt collector rules under the FDCPA
- [RCW 26.16.030](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=26.16.030) — Washington's community property statute
- [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/) — Additional consumer protections around debt collection

---

*Handling an estate involves more than just debt. [Answer a few questions](/survey/death) and After Atlas will build a personalized checklist covering everything relevant to your situation.*

articles.title: How to Manage a Loved One's Digital Accounts and Online Assets After Death
articles.metaTitle: Managing a Loved One's Digital Assets After Death
articles.metaDescription: A practical guide to handling email, cloud storage, cryptocurrency, and payment apps after someone dies — including what to do if you don't have the password.
articles.body:
A generation ago, "settling an estate" meant paperwork, keys, and physical property. Today it also means email accounts, cloud photo libraries, cryptocurrency wallets, and payment apps — and most of these don't come with a clear instruction manual for what to do when the account holder has died. Here's a practical breakdown by account type.

## Why this category is different from the rest of the checklist

Most tasks after a death — closing a bank account, canceling a subscription — follow an established process, because financial institutions deal with deaths constantly. Digital accounts are newer territory: policies vary widely between companies, and some accounts (particularly cryptocurrency) may be genuinely unrecoverable without specific information the account holder had.

## Email and cloud storage

Email is often the master key to everything else — many other accounts use it for password resets, so it's worth prioritizing.

- **If you have the password**, you can typically log in directly, though check the provider's terms first — accessing someone else's account, even a deceased relative's, can technically violate some providers' terms of service without going through their official process.
- **If you don't have the password**, most major providers (Google, Microsoft, Apple, Yahoo) have a formal legacy or deceased-user process, usually requiring a death certificate and proof of your relationship or executor status. These processes exist specifically for this situation — see [Apple's Legacy Contact process](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102631) and [Google's Inactive Account Manager](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546) for the two most common examples.
- **Cloud storage and photos** (Google Photos, iCloud, Dropbox) are often tied to the same account as email, so resolving email access frequently resolves this too.

## Cryptocurrency

This is the account type most likely to be permanently lost, and it's worth understanding why before you start searching.

- Cryptocurrency held in a **personal wallet** (not an exchange) is typically accessible only with the private key or seed phrase. If the deceased didn't record this somewhere and share it, the funds may be genuinely unrecoverable — there's no customer service line to call, since it's not held by any company.
- Cryptocurrency held on an **exchange** (like Coinbase) works more like a traditional financial account — the exchange typically has a documented process for next of kin, similar to a bank.
- If you're searching for crypto holdings you suspect exist but can't locate, check for hardware wallets (small USB-like devices), written seed phrases in a safe or safe deposit box, and password manager entries.

## Payment apps with a balance

PayPal, Venmo, Cash App, and similar apps often hold real money and have their own next-of-kin or estate claim processes, generally requiring a death certificate. Check each app's support documentation directly, since specific requirements vary and change over time.

## Social media accounts

Most major platforms offer two options: **memorialization** (the account remains visible, often with a note indicating the person has passed, and can't be logged into) or **deletion**, upon request with proof of death. Which is appropriate is a personal and family decision — some families find a memorialized account meaningful, others find it painful to encounter.

## Domain names and monetized content

If the deceased owned a website domain, ran a blog, or had a monetized YouTube channel or similar, these have real (sometimes significant) value and their own transfer processes through the registrar or platform — this is easy to overlook amid everything else, but worth including on your list if it applies.

## A practical starting point

1. **Make a list of accounts** you know or suspect existed — check the person's email inbox for account confirmations and password reset emails, which often reveal accounts you didn't know about
2. **Check for a password manager** — if the deceased used one, it may be the single fastest way to access everything at once
3. **Prioritize accounts holding money** (crypto, payment apps, brokerage) over accounts holding sentimental value (photos, social media) if you're working with limited time or energy
4. **Keep a death certificate on hand** — nearly every formal digital-asset process requires one

This is just one category of a larger checklist. For everything else that needs handling after a death, see [our complete first-30-days guide](/blog/what-to-do-after-someone-dies-checklist).

## Frequently asked questions

**What happens to someone's email if no one has the password?**
Major providers have a formal process for next of kin or an executor to request access or account closure, typically requiring a death certificate. Response times and exact requirements vary by provider.

**Can I access a deceased person's cryptocurrency without their password?**
Only if it's held on an exchange, which has its own account-recovery process. Cryptocurrency in a personal, self-custodied wallet generally cannot be recovered without the private key or seed phrase — there's no company to contact.

**Should I memorialize or delete a deceased person's social media account?**
There's no universally right answer — it's a personal decision, and different family members may feel differently about it. Most platforms let you choose either option with proof of death.

## Sources

- [Apple Support — How to add a Legacy Contact](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102631)
- [Google — Inactive Account Manager](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546)

---

*Digital assets are one piece of a much larger picture. [Answer a few questions](/survey/death) and After Atlas will build a checklist covering everything relevant to your specific situation.*

articles.title: How to Support Grieving Children After the Death of a Family Member
articles.metaTitle: How to Support Grieving Children After a Death
articles.metaDescription: Age-by-age guidance for talking to children about death, answering their questions honestly, and recognizing when a child may need extra support.
articles.body:
While the adults in a family are working through funeral arrangements, paperwork, and their own grief, children in the household are processing the same loss — often without the words or context to make sense of it. Here's practical, age-informed guidance for supporting them through it.

## Start with honest, simple language

It's a natural instinct to soften the news, but euphemisms like "went to sleep" or "went away" can genuinely confuse young children and, in some cases, create fear around ordinary sleep or travel. Clear, simple, honest language tends to serve children better:

> "Grandpa's body stopped working, and he died. That means we won't see him anymore, and it's really sad. It's okay to feel sad, and it's okay to ask me anything about it."

Use the words "died" and "death" directly rather than avoiding them — children pick up on avoidance, and it can signal that the topic is too frightening or shameful to discuss openly, which tends to make things harder, not easier.

## What to expect by age

This is generally consistent with guidance from child bereavement organizations like the [National Alliance for Children's Grief](https://nacg.org/):

**Young children (roughly 2–6):** Death is often understood as temporary or reversible at this age — a child might ask when the person is coming back, more than once, even after being told. This isn't defiance or a sign something's wrong; it reflects how young children's understanding of permanence develops. Expect the same questions to come up repeatedly.

**School-age children (roughly 6–12):** Children in this range generally understand that death is permanent and can experience grief more similarly to adults, including sadness, anger, and anxiety about other people they love dying too. They may also ask very direct, sometimes startling questions ("what happens to the body?") — these are usually genuine curiosity, not a cause for alarm.

**Teenagers:** Adolescents often grieve more like adults but may be less likely to bring it up unprompted, sometimes processing it more with peers than family, or appearing to cope by staying busy. Checking in periodically, without pressuring them to talk, tends to work better than waiting for them to initiate.

## Keep routines as steady as possible

Amid funeral planning and family upheaval, maintaining school schedules, mealtimes, and bedtimes gives children a sense of stability precisely when everything else feels uncertain. This doesn't mean shielding them from the loss — it means giving them a predictable structure to process it within.

## Let them be part of it, on their terms

Children often benefit from being included in family rituals — attending a funeral or memorial, if they want to and are prepared for what to expect beforehand, or contributing something like a drawing or a memory to share. Forcing participation isn't necessary or helpful, but excluding children entirely can leave them feeling shut out of something the rest of the family is going through together.

## Expect grief to look different than you'd expect

Children often grieve in bursts rather than continuously — deeply sad one moment, playing normally the next. This is developmentally typical, not a sign that they don't understand or don't care. Regression in younger children (bedwetting, clinginess, trouble sleeping) is also common and usually temporary.

## When to seek additional support

Most children move through grief with time, honesty, and steady support from the adults around them. It may be worth involving a child therapist or grief counselor if you notice, over an extended period:

- Persistent difficulty functioning at school or with friends
- Ongoing physical symptoms without a clear cause
- Expressions of guilt that the child somehow caused the death
- Signs the child is being asked to become the emotional caretaker of grieving adults, rather than the other way around

Many communities have grief support groups specifically for children, often run through hospice organizations or children's hospitals, which can be a valuable complement to family support.

## Taking care of yourself matters too

Children are often more affected by how the adults around them are coping than by the loss itself. Getting support for your own grief — from friends, family, or a counselor — isn't separate from supporting your children through theirs; it's part of it.

For everything else that needs handling after a death, see [our complete first-30-days checklist](/blog/what-to-do-after-someone-dies-checklist).

## Frequently asked questions

**Should I bring my child to the funeral?**
Generally yes, if the child wants to go and understands beforehand what to expect — but it should be their choice where possible, not a requirement.

**Is it normal for my child to seem unaffected?**
Yes — children often grieve in short bursts rather than continuously, and appearing to move on quickly doesn't mean the loss hasn't registered.

**How do I answer questions I don't have answers to, like what happens after death?**
It's okay to say you don't know, and to share what you personally believe if that feels right for your family — children generally respond better to honest uncertainty than to answers that feel evasive.

## Sources

- [National Alliance for Children's Grief](https://nacg.org/) — Education and resources for supporting grieving children and teens
- [NAEYC — Helping Young Children Grieve and Understand Death](https://www.naeyc.org/resources/pubs/yc/may2019/helping-young-children-grieve) — Developmental perspective on children's understanding of death

---

*Supporting a grieving family involves more than emotional care. [Answer a few questions](/survey/death) and After Atlas will help you build a checklist for everything else that needs handling.*
